issue.title: git entities per commit vs per time window

labels.name: module:collaboration_network
labels.description: Issues related to collaboration network construction, parsing and metrics.

issue.body:
It appears performing git blame per commit can be too expensive for projects with 44k commits+, such as OpenSSL. This limitation is noted in [Joblin's dissertation](https://www.infosun.fim.uni-passau.de/spl/theses/MitchellJoblinDiss.pdf) Section 2.2, page 18:

> By grouping the commits together, only the project state for the ﬁrst and last commit needs to be reconstructed.

, and Codeface code:

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/VCS.py#L1140-L1146

We should reimplement the removed line_type that scans a folder, and combine with`git_checkout()`.

issue.title: Extract graph model and implement OSLOM community detection interface

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: type:refactoring
labels.description: Code changes that improve maintenability, performance, etc

issue.body:
As new networks were coded, R/network.R grew to have too many duplicated ways to create a graph with data. The SNAP Stanford library distinguishes networks and graphs operations, which served as an inspiration to do so here as well. 

Defining R/graph.R to separate graph operations, and subsequently associating algorithm and metrics to graphs, rather than network, should keep the codebase much saner for the long run.

issue.title: Transition to OO R6 Class System

labels.name: type:wontfix
labels.description: This will not be worked on

labels.name: type:refactoring
labels.description: Code changes that improve maintenability, performance, etc

labels.name: type:milestone
labels.description: Issues representing milestones since they don't recognize markdown...

issue.body:
This is something I've been debating on to transition sooner than later.

[R6 Class](https://github.com/r-lib/R6) basically is one of the ways R implements object-oriented design, which is the closest to how Python and Java have it. 

[A quick tutorial from the Advanced R book which would take someone 5-10 minutes to learn](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/r6.html) suffices to enable this codebase to, at least have:

 * Classes with attributes and methods.
 * Class Inheritance 
 * Private and Public Methods. 

This concern came around for two reasons for the long run: Tables in any format flying around, and functions. 

# Code Interfaces - E.g.: The Churn Function

The churn function is defined like so:

```r
# git_log is a data.table, where each row is identified by a commit. It must contain
# 4 columns in any order but with these column names: commit_hash, date, added, removed.
metric_commit_interval_churn <- function(git_log,start_commit,end_commit){

  git_log$churn <- metric_churn(git_log$added,git_log$removed)
  # Calculate Churn per Commit
.
.
.
}
```

As can be seen above, I have no means to enforce any expectation of the table column names and what it should like. 

An alternative to this would be to require the object passed to be "as output from `parse_gitlog()`. However, if parse_gitlog() evolves to use different parsers, I must list all functions that output from said function.  

There may also be situations where it is desirable to add more information to the table in any particular order. In the future, we may want to add not only churn but issue data (bug / not bug). Adding or removing columns to the table does not affect metric_churn().

milestone.title: 0.0.0.9000 Recreate Smells Study Analysis
milestone.description: The existing analysis is no longer runnable. See #17 for details.

issue.body:
The purpose of this issue is to understand how can a dev-file network can be obtained at function granularity. The following links are cues to that. A more organized analysis is done in further comments. 

This file from Codeface employs ctags:

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/cluster/cluster.py#L1414

Exuberant Ctags basically is a parser that takes as input a source file (e.g. bla.py) and outputs metadata of functions and other data objects of said source code as another file. Making sense of the metadata file appears to be very confusing, see this question on SO:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41933837/understanding-the-ctags-file-format

However, Codeface relies on a python library to parse Ctags, making it much simpler. This implementation appears to be very efficient, as it seems to be just a wrapper to a C file that does the parsing (notice the github project hasn't be updated in a long while):

https://github.com/cloggo/python-ctags

Codeface also relies on this VCS python package, which appears to abstract implementations of version control systems (Git, Subversion):

https://github.com/codeinn/vcs

Lastly, I also found out Exuberant Ctags itself has been abandoned, and other project took over forking it since then: 

https://ctags.io/

issue.title: Networks in Kaiaulu and 3rd party dependencies

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: priority:future
labels.description: For issues which will be deferred / wishlist

labels.name: module:graph
labels.description: Issues related to the graph module

issue.body:
Currently, Kaiaulu has a really ad-hoc implementation of [networks](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/master/R/network.R) (i.e. it represents in a list nodes and edges tables, each being a data.table). The definition grew organically to use the visualizations provided by vizNetwork for exploration early on, but it doesn't make sense to, from here onwards, re-code an entire network library. 

In Codeface4Smells, the Smells were built on top of igraph and leverages its bipartite projection algorithms. However, doing so here would automatically re-license the codebase from MPL 2.0 to GPL. Moreover, it is hard to believe igraph is the only library available out there.

This issue is a small survey of existing tools found "in the wild" for consideration, not only based on the license but on features, etc, and for reflection on how far we need to go in regards to dependencies. Generally, I would prefer to not consider such a core data model and functionality of the package dependent on anything (unless it is incorporated directly to the codebase and doesn't cost setup overhead).

issue.title: Replace explict calls of POSIXct and time arithmetic by stringi_datetime

labels.name: type:refactoring
labels.description: Code changes that improve maintenability, performance, etc

issue.body:
I recently became aware that, among its large API, stringi also provides functions to [format strings into POSIXct objects](http://www.gagolewski.com/software/stringi/manual/?manpage=stri_datetime_format), and time arithmetic (see: [stri_datetime_*](http://www.gagolewski.com/software/stringi/manual/) functions). 

For consistency, direct calls to POSIXct should be replaced by the associated calls in stringi, which Kaiaulu already imports and extensively use for string manipulation.

issue.title: Good CLI for R Packages

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: type:interoperability
labels.description: For code that interfaces with third party applications

issue.body: Call today with Jason made me reconsider the merits of CLI for packages in being more ubiquitous as a trade-off for rigidity, so others can leverage the package functionality in a language they are more comfortable with. This is on the same vein as #65, but it serves as a way to "default to" if not using Python or R.
